sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Xīwángmǔ** (*xiwangmu*) ​— Queen Mother ‌of the West ‌· Western queen mother ​— belongs to ​the Daoist tradition, ​where it is ​catalogued under the ​domain "Queen Mother ‌of the West". ​The name means "Western ​queen mother"[^1].

**Xīwángmǔ**, ‌the Queen Mother ​of the West, ‌has the strangest ​biography of any ‌great goddess in ​the Chinese tradition. Her ​oldest portrait, in ​the *Classic of ​Mountains and Seas*, ​is fearsome: a ‌figure with a ​tiger's teeth and ‌a leopard's tail, her ​hair wild, wearing ‌the *shèng* headdress, ​presiding over plague ‌and calamity from ​Mount Kūnlún at ‌the western edge of ​the world. She ​is not yet ‌the serene sovereign ‌of later ages ‌— she is ​the numinous power ​of the untamed west ‌itself.

Across the ​Han dynasty she ​was refined, age ‌by age, into ​the great goddess ​of the western ‌paradise: keeper of the ​Peaches of Immortality, ‌which ripen once ​every three thousand ​years; host of ​the Peach Banquet; ​bestower of the ‌elixir that lifts Cháng'é ‌to the moon; ​and, in the ‌fullness of Taoist ​theology, the sovereign ​of yin and ‌the west, balanced ‌against Dōngwánggōng, the King ‌Father of the ‌East. The wilderness ​was never banished ‌from her — ​it was enthroned.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores the name ​as **Xīwángmǔ** and ‌serves its temple ​at [xīwángmǔ.com](https://xn--xwngm-yqa03cy7b.com). The ​restoration preserves at ​least one distinctive ‌feature — a ​diacritic or a distinctive ​letter — that ​the ASCII form ‌loses, and exactly ​one historically valid ‌Unicode restoration exists, ​which places the ‌name in Tier 1. ​The plain ASCII ‌form *xiwangmu* survives ‌as a modern ​convenience imposed by ​the early domain-name ​system; the restoration, ​not the fallback, is ‌the form the ‌project defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Shan Hai Jing (Classic of Mountains and Seas).
Huainanzi, Liu An; Chinese Text Project, 139 BCE.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Chinese characters ​as **西王母**. ​Etymologically it ​means "Western ​queen mother"[^1].

​The ASCII ‌form ​*xiwangmu* survives ​only because ‌the early ​domain-name system ‌could not ​carry diacritics; ‌it is ​a technological ​compromise, ​not an ​ancient spelling. ​The Unicode ‌restoration **Xīwángmǔ** ​recovers both ‌the stress ​accent and ‌the ​vowel length ‌of the ​original directly ‌in the ​address bar. ​The restoration ‌preserves at ‌least one ‌distinctive ​feature — ​a diacritic ‌or a ​distinctive letter ​— that ‌the ASCII ​form loses, ​and exactly ‌one ​historically valid ‌Unicode restoration ​exists, which ​places the ​name in ​Tier 1.

‌The letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

​- ‌**x** → ​**X** — ​Same, capitalized
‌- **i** ‌→ **ī** ‌— Long ‌vowel
- ​**w** → ‌**w** ​— Same
​- **a** ​→ **á** ‌— Stress ​on a
​- **n** ​→ **n** ‌— ​Same
- ​**g** → ​**g** — ‌Same
- ​**m** → ‌**m** — ​Same
- ‌**u** → ​**ǔ** ‌— Special ‌character

The ​project holds ​the domain ​**xīwángmǔ.com** (xn--xwngm-yqa03cy7b.com) ​as the ‌canonical home ‌of this ​name[^2].

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of the ‌name is **/ɕi˥ ‌waŋ˧˥ mu˨˩˦/** — ​Modern Standard Mandarin ​(Pinyin).[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

- ​**xī** — Voiceless ​alveolo-palatal fricative [ɕ] ‌followed by high ​front vowel [i], ​Tone 1 (high ‌level, ˥). Pinyin ​'x' has no ‌English equivalent; it ​is the 'sh' ‌of 'she' ​pushed forward toward ​the teeth.
- ​**wáng** — Labial-velar ​approximant [w] with ​the final [aŋ] ‌(open central vowel ​+ velar nasal), ‌Tone 2 (rising, ​˧˥).
- **mǔ** ‌— Bilabial nasal ​[m] with ‌high back rounded ​vowel [u], Tone ‌3 (dipping, ˨˩˦) ​— the low, ​dipping contour that ‌falls before it ‌rises.

For the ‌modern speaker, the ​closest approximation is: ​shee-WAHNG-moo — Xī ‌held high ​and level like ​a sustained note, ‌wáng rising from ​mid to high ​as in a ‌question, mǔ dipping ​low and turning ‌up again.

Kindred ​and historical forms ​of the name:

​- **Traditional** ​— 西王母
- ‌**Simplified** — 西王母
‌- **Wade-Giles** — ​Hsi¹-wang²-mu³
- **Her ‌consort** — 東王公 ​Dōngwánggōng (King Father ​of the East)
‌- **Related terms** ‌— 蟠桃 pántáo ‌(Peaches of Immortality); ‌蟠桃會 pántáohuì ​(the Peach Banquet); ‌崑崙 Kūnlún (her ​western mountain)

西王母 ​means 'Queen Mother ​of the West' ‌— xī (west), ​wáng (king, sovereign), ​mǔ (mother). The ​Modern Standard Mandarin ‌reading is Xīwángmǔ ​(Tones 1-2-3), ​as recorded in ​the Unihan Database ‌(Unicode Consortium, kMandarin) ​and standard Mandarin ‌dictionaries. The tone-marked ​Pinyin restoration Xīwángmǔ ‌preserves the citation ​tones of all ‌three syllables; in ‌connected speech the ​third tone ​on mǔ is ​often realized as ​a low half-third ‌tone, but the ‌lexical tone remains ​Tone 3.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌written in ‌Chinese characters ​as **西王母**. ​This ​original script ​is the ​form against ‌which ​the ASCII ​fallback *xiwangmu* ‌and the ​PuniCodex restoration ‌**Xīwángmǔ** ​are measured: ‌the restoration ​preserves both ​its pitch ​accent ​and its ​vowel quantity ‌of the ​written ‌form, so ​that a ‌reader typing ​the modern ‌address ​still speaks ‌the ancient ​name.[^1]

The ​original ‌script is ‌西王母, written ‌identically in ​traditional and ​simplified ‌characters — ​none of ​the three ‌graphs was ​altered ​in the ‌twentieth-century simplification. ​Pinyin *Xīwángmǔ* ‌(Tones ​1-2-3) is ​the Modern ​Standard Mandarin ​reading, recorded ‌in ‌the Unihan ​Database and ‌standard dictionaries: ​xī (west, ​Tone ‌1), wáng ‌(sovereign, Tone ‌2), mǔ ‌(mother, ​Tone 3). ‌The registrable ​Unicode restoration ​uses the ​tone-marked ‌Pinyin rather ​than the ​hanzi because ​PUNICODEX ‌renders the ​original characters ​in the ​temple's 'Original ‌Script' ​card while ‌keeping the ​domain label ‌pronounceable and ​internationally ‌registrable; the ‌tone marks ​ī, á, ​and ​ǔ carry ​the citation ‌tones that ‌plain ASCII ​drops.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Xīwángmǔ**, the ​Queen Mother of ‌the West, has the ‌strangest biography of ​any great goddess ​in the Chinese tradition. ​Her oldest portrait, ​in the *Classic ​of Mountains and ‌Seas*, is fearsome: a ​figure with a ​tiger's teeth and ‌a leopard's tail, her ​hair wild, wearing ‌the *shèng* headdress, ​presiding over plague ‌and calamity from Mount ​Kūnlún at the ​western edge of ​the world. She is ​not yet the ​serene sovereign of ‌later ages — ​she is the numinous ‌power of the ​untamed west itself.

‌Across the Han dynasty ​she was refined, ‌age by age, ​into the great ‌goddess of the western ​paradise: keeper of ​the Peaches of ‌Immortality, which ripen once ‌every three thousand ‌years; host of ​the Peach Banquet; ​bestower of the elixir ‌that lifts Cháng'é ​to the moon; ​and, in the fullness ‌of Taoist theology, ​the sovereign of ​yin and the ‌west, balanced against Dōngwánggōng, ​the King Father ‌of the East. ​The wilderness was ​never banished from her ​— it was ​enthroned.[^1]

### Mount ‌Kūnlún

Her paradise stands ‌on Mount Kūnlún ​at the western ‌edge of the ​world, the axis where ​heaven leans down ‌to meet the ‌wild earth.

### The ‌Peaches of Immortality

‌The pántáo ripen ​once every three ‌thousand years; to taste ​one is to ​step outside death's ​jurisdiction — which is ‌why the Monkey ​King could not ​resist them.

### ​Tiger's Teeth, Leopard's Tail

‌Her archaic form ​keeps its claws: ​the Shān Hǎi Jīng ​gives her a ‌tiger's teeth and ​a leopard's tail, ‌the regalia of a ​mistress of plague ‌and calamity.

### ​Sovereign of Yin and ‌the West

In ‌mature Taoist theology ​she rules yin, ​the west, and all ​goddesses, balanced against ​Dōngwánggōng's yang and ‌east — the two ‌poles of a ​complete cosmos.

sources.citation: Huainanzi, Liu An; Chinese Text Project, 139 BCE.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography associated ‌with ‌Xīwángmǔ concentrates ​in ​a ​small set ​of ​recurring attributes, ‌each ​a compressed ​statement ‌about the ​name:[^1]

‌- **The ​shèng ‌headdress** ​— Her ​ancient ​insignia of ​authority ​— the ‌distinctive ​headdress she ‌wears ​even in ‌her ​oldest, ‌wildest images
​- ‌**Tiger's teeth ​and ​leopard's tail** ‌— ‌The zoomorphic ‌vestiges ​of her ​primordial ‌form, ​marking her ​dominion ‌over plague ​and ​calamity
- ‌**The ​Peaches of ‌Immortality** ​— Sovereignty ​over ​death ​itself — ‌fruit ‌that ripens ​once ‌in three ​thousand ​years and ‌frees ‌the eater ‌from ‌mortality
​- **Mount ‌Kūnlún** ​— The ​western ​paradise at ‌the ​edge of ​the ​world, where ‌her ​palace ​and orchards ​stand
‌- **The ​tallies** ‌— The ​tokens ‌her Han-era ​devotees ‌carried from ‌commandery ​to ​commandery as ​pledges ​of her ‌protection ‌and long ​life

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Xīwángmǔ's myths trace ​an arc no other Chinese ‌deity matches: from wilderness terror ‌to the most gracious sovereign ​of the Taoist heavens. Each ​age kept something of ​the last, so that the ​serene hostess of the Peach ​Banquet still carries the teeth ‌and tail of the mountain ​power she once was.[^1]

### ​The Fearsome Portrait (Shan Hai ‌Jing)

In the *Classic of ​Mountains and Seas*, the oldest ‌surviving description, the Queen Mother ​is not a queen ‌at all in the courtly ​sense. She has a tiger's ​teeth and a leopard's tail, ​her hair unbound beneath the ​*shèng* headdress, and she presides ​over plague and calamity from ‌Mount Kūnlún. She is the ​personified danger of the far ‌west — the lands ​beyond the pale of the ‌settled world, where the sun ​goes down into mystery. Later ‌ages would clothe her in ​silk, but the earliest text ‌keeps her wild.[^2]

### The ​Elixir for Hòuyì (Huainanzi)

It ​is the Queen Mother who ‌holds the elixir of immortality, ‌and it is she ‌who grants it to Hòuyì, ​the archer who shot down ​the nine excess suns. The ‌gift does not stay in ​his hands: it becomes Cháng'é's ​ascension to the moon. The ‌versions differ — in some ​tellings Cháng'é takes the elixir ​unbidden, in others to keep ‌it from unworthy hands ​— but the constant is ‌the source: immortality flows from ​the Queen Mother's store, and ​no one rises to the ​heavens except through her treasury.

​### The Theft of the ‌Peaches (Journey to the West)

‌Once every three thousand years ​the Peaches of Immortality ripen, ‌and the Queen Mother ​hosts the *Peach Banquet* for ​the assembled immortals. In the ‌*Journey to the West*, Sūn ‌Wùkōng — appointed, with fatal ‌optimism, as guardian of the ‌orchard — eats his way ​through the finest fruit and ‌crashes the feast he was ​never invited to. It is ​one of literature's great ​heists, and its comedy rests ‌on a real theological point: ​the peaches are the most ​tightly held treasure in heaven, ​and the Queen Mother is ‌their unanswerable custodian.

### The ​Movement of 3 BCE (Book ​of Han)

The Queen Mother ​was not only a ‌figure of elite texts and ​palace mirrors. The *Book of ‌Han* records a genuine millenarian ​movement in 3 BCE, when ‌crowds across the commanderies carried ​her tallies, passed them from ‌hand to hand, and awaited ‌the fulfilment of her promise. ​It is one of the ​earliest documented popular religious ​movements in Chinese history — ​proof that the western goddess ‌had seized the imagination of ‌ordinary people centuries before the ​novelists found her.

sources.citation: Huainanzi, Liu An; Chinese Text Project, 139 BCE.
Han Shu (Book of Han).

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
The ​Queen Mother ‌travelled with ‌Chinese letters ​and liturgy ​across East ​Asia. In ​Japan she ​is read ‌*Seiōbo*, ​appearing in ​painting, garden ‌imagery, and ​the literary ‌imagination as ​the hostess ‌of the ​western orchard; ​in ​Korea she ​is *Seowangmo*, ​present in ‌folklore and ​shamanic song; ‌in Vietnamese ​she is ‌*Tây ​Vương Mẫu*, ‌her name ​borne into ‌the southern ​reception of ​the Taoist ‌pantheon. Within ‌China her ‌deepest ​transformation was ​her absorption ‌into organized ​Taoism, where ​she rose ‌to the ​summit of ​the celestial ‌hierarchy ​as sovereign ‌of yin ​and the ​west, paired ​with Dōngwánggōng, ​the King ‌Father of ‌the East, ​as ‌the balanced ​poles of ​the cosmos. ‌Buddhist storytellers ‌did not ‌so much ‌absorb her ​as borrow ‌her ​orchard: the ​immortality peaches ​and the ‌great banquet ​pass freely ​between Taoist ​and popular-Buddhist ‌narrative ​worlds, and ​it is ​in that ‌shared space ​that the ‌*Journey to ​the West* ‌stages her ​most ‌famous scene.[^1]

‌Within the ​Daoist tradition, ​closely related ​names in ​the corpus ‌include [[laozi|Lǎozǐ]], ‌[[wuji|Wújí]], and ​[[yinyang|Yīnyáng]].

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: The ​Queen Mother ‌never retired ‌from ​the heavens. ​In Taoist ​temples ​across Taiwan ​and the ‌diaspora ​she is ​venerated still, ‌often under ​the ‌title Golden ​Mother of ‌the ​Jasper Pool, ​and her ​birthday ​is kept ​with festival ‌observance. ​In art ‌she rides ​phoenixes ‌and cranes ​through centuries ‌of ​painting, lacquer, ‌and embroidery, ​and ​the immortal ‌peach she ‌tends became ‌the ​standard emblem ​of longevity, ‌pressed ​into birthday ​buns and ‌painted ​onto porcelain ​as a ‌wish ​for long ‌life. The ​*Journey ​to the ​West* made ​her ‌banquet immortal ‌in another ​sense: ‌every screen ​adaptation of ​the Monkey ‌King's ‌career — ‌film, television, ‌animation, ​games — ‌must sooner ​or ​later raid ​her orchard. ‌She ​remains what ​she has ​been ‌since the ​Han mirrors ​first ​invoked her ‌for blessing: ​the ‌great goddess ​at the ‌western edge ​of ‌the world, ‌holding the ​one ​treasure every ​mortal wants ​and ‌no one ‌may take ​uninvited.[^1]

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: The ​Queen Mother's ‌earliest ‌textual portrait ​is in ​the ​*Classic of ​Mountains ​and Seas*, ‌compiled from ​Warring ​States through ‌Han ​materials (roughly ‌4th–1st centuries ​BCE), ‌where she ​appears ​with tiger's ​teeth and ​a ​leopard's tail ‌on ​Mount Kūnlún. ‌Her ​great material ‌flourishing is ​Han: ‌bronze mirrors ​invoke ‌her by ​name for ​blessing ‌and long ‌life, ‌and tomb ​reliefs and ​murals ‌— most ​famously ​the Wu ‌Liang shrine ​of ​the 2nd ‌century ​CE — ‌show ​her enthroned ​in the ​west, ​increasingly paired ‌with ‌Dōngwánggōng in ​the east. ‌The ​*Book of ​Han* ‌preserves the ‌documentary trace ‌of ‌her popular ​cult ‌in the ​millenarian movement ​of ​3 BCE, ‌when ​her tallies ​passed ​through the ‌commanderies. By ​the ​medieval period, ​Taoist ‌scriptures and ​liturgical texts ‌had ​raised her ‌to ​the summit ‌of the ‌goddess ​hierarchy, the ​form ​in which ​she has ‌been ‌worshipped ever ​since.[^1]

sections.label: Yijing & Hexagrams
sections.body: The ​Queen ‌Mother ‌is the ​*Yijing*'s ​west ​made ​personal. ​The ‌oracle's ​spatial grammar ​assigns ‌the ​west ‌to ​autumn, ‌metal, ​and the ​yin ​half ​of ​the ‌year; ​hexagram ‌2, *Kūn* ​坤 ‌— ​six ‌broken ​lines, ‌pure receptive ​yin, ​'the ‌mare' ‌— ‌names ​the ​feminine earth-principle ‌she ​rules, ​and ‌the ​trigram ​*Duì* ‌兌, the ​joyous ‌lake ​of ​the ​west, ​is ‌her palace's ‌emblem ​in ‌later ​cosmographic ​reading.[^1] ‌Medieval ‌speculation completed ‌the ‌symmetry: ​as ‌*Kūn* ​answers ​*Qián*, the ​Queen ‌Mother ​of ​the ​West ‌was ​paired with ​the ​King ‌Father ​of ‌the ​East ‌(Dōngwánggōng), yin ​sovereign ‌to ‌his ​yang ​— ​the ​hexagrams' parents ‌enthroned ‌as ​gods.[^2]

sources.citation: Yijing (Zhouyi), hexagram 2 Kūn; trigram Duì.

sections.label: Inner Alchemy (Neidan)
sections.body: Inner ​alchemy ‌claimed ‌the Queen ​Mother ​as ​its ​own ​ancestress. ‌The ​elixir she ​hands ‌[[houyi|Hòuyì]] ​in ‌the ​*Huáinánzǐ* ‌is ​the outer ​form ​of ​what ​neidan ‌refines ​within: ‌lead and ​mercury, ‌dragon ​and ‌tiger, ​joined ‌under a ​western ​yin ‌sovereign ‌to ‌produce ​the ​deathless embryo.[^1] ‌The ​pairing ​with ‌the ​King ​Father ‌of the ​East ‌became ​the ​alchemical ​diagram ​of ‌cosmic intercourse ‌internalized ​— ‌the ​practitioner ​stages ‌their ‌union in ‌the ‌dantian ​rather ‌than ​on ​Kūnlún. The ​female-alchemy ‌(nǚdan) ​lineages ​of ​the ‌Qing ​went further, ​tracing ​their ‌transmission ​directly ‌to ​her: ‌the sovereign ​of ‌all ‌female ​transcendents ​teaching ​women ​the refinement ‌she ‌herself ​embodies.[^2]

sources.citation: Huáinánzǐ, elixir narrative; neidan cosmology.
Despeux & Kohn, Women in Daoism (Three Pines Press, 2003), on nǚdan lineages.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Xīwángmǔ ​teaches that ‌civilization ‌does not ​destroy its ​wilderness; ​it enthrones ​it. ​The tiger-toothed ‌power ​of the ​Shān Hǎi ‌Jīng ​was not ‌replaced ​by the ‌serene ​hostess of ​the Peach ​Banquet ​— she ​was ‌carried forward, ​wildness ‌and all, ​into ‌the highest ​seat of ‌the ​Taoist heavens. ‌The ​goddess who ​once ‌sent plague ‌became the ‌goddess ​who grants ​endless ‌life, and ​the ​two offices ‌are not ​as ​far apart ‌as ​they seem: ‌both ​are sovereignty ​over the ​boundary ​between life ‌and ‌death, held ​by ‌the same ​unanswerable hand.

​To ‌name a ‌domain ‌*Xīwángmǔ* is ‌to ​claim that ‌whole arc ​— ​the west ​where ‌the sun ​descends, ​the orchard ​where ‌three thousand ​years ripen ​into ​a single ‌fruit, ​and the ‌promise ​whispered from ‌tally to ​tally ‌through the ‌Han ​commanderies: that ​mortality ​is a ​border, and ‌someone ‌keeps the ​gate.[^1]

sources.citation: Shan Hai Jing (Classic of Mountains and Seas).
